nodes.label: The African Neolithic
nodes.full: The Nile Valley and eastern Sahara: the wider world of the cattle cult, the source of sorghum and the summer-crop package, and the ceramic tradition (the Gash Group) that Tihama pottery echoes across the Red Sea.
nodes.src: background — added on review; Boivin and Fuller, Journal of World Prehistory 22 (2009); Manzo on Red Sea interaction.

nodes.label: The Horn of Africa
nodes.full: The Ethiopian highlands and the African shore of the Bab al-Mandab: the other half of the obsidian exchange and the ceramic interaction sphere, twenty miles across the strait.
nodes.src: background — Khalidi, 'Holocene obsidian exchange in the Red Sea region' (2010).

nodes.label: The kingdom of Sabaʾ
nodes.full: The literate caravan state that forms in the highlands around Marib after 1200 BC: it inherits highland runoff irrigation and scales it into the Marib Dam, and its rise coincides with the emptying of the coastal town of Sabir.
nodes.src: background — added on review; forward reference to the planned successor folio south-arabia-1200bc-300bc.

nodes.label: Holocene herders enter the southern highlands
nodes.full: As the early Holocene monsoon pushed rain deep into the south, foraging groups and the first cattle-, sheep- and goat-herders spread across the Yemen highlands and the perennial wadis of the Hadramawt. This is the population whose descendants would build the cattle monuments and, three thousand years later, the terraced villages.
nodes.src: the RASA (Roots of Agriculture in Southern Arabia / AHSD) project, McCorriston and Harrower; the Dhamar Survey Project, Wilkinson, Edens and Gibson, 'Sabaean irrigated agriculture... the central highlands of Yemen', Antiquity / AAE (1999).

nodes.label: Manayzah rockshelter, Wadi Sana
nodes.full: The stratified deposits at Manayzah hold the earliest securely dated domestic cattle, sheep and goat in southern Arabia, alongside the fine pressure-flaked points of the Arabian bifacial tradition. It is the anchor site for the region's Neolithic chronology.
nodes.src: McCorriston, Harrower et al., RASA project excavation reports; Crassard on the Manayzah lithic sequence, 'Wadi Sana and the Neolithic of Hadramawt', Arabian Archaeology and Epigraphy.

nodes.label: The turret tombs of the Hadramawt plateau
nodes.full: Thousands of drystone 'High Circular Tombs' line the ridgelines of the Hadramawt plateau, built and reused over two millennia by mobile pastoralists. Placed to be seen from the valleys below, they map a segmentary society onto the landscape without a single settlement or ruler's name.
nodes.src: RASA project tomb surveys; earlier recording by the Soviet-Yemeni Complex Expedition (Sedov, Griaznevich). Harrower and McCorriston, 'Ancient territories... the Hadramawt', in the RASA synthesis volumes.

nodes.label: The Kheshiya cattle-skull monument
nodes.full: On a low rise in Wadi Sana, herders laid out a ring of some forty cattle crania in a single act, brought from many different herds and buried together. It is the oldest monumental construction known in South Arabia and the clearest sign of supra-household cooperation before the historic kingdoms.
nodes.src: McCorriston, Harrower, Martin et al., 'Cattle cults of the Arabian Neolithic and early territorial societies', American Anthropologist 114 (2012).

nodes.label: The Bronze Age culture of Khawlan at-Tiyal
nodes.full: The Italian Archaeological Mission found a network of small drystone villages in the highlands east of Sanaa — permanent houses, terraced fields, storage and a settled domestic assemblage. This 'Khawlan Bronze Age' is the first evidence of village life in the Yemeni highlands and the immediate ancestor of the Sabaean settlement pattern.
nodes.src: Alessandro de Maigret (ed.), 'The Bronze Age Culture of Hawlan at-Tiyal and al-Hada (Republic of Yemen)', IsMEO, Rome (1990).

nodes.label: The Dhamar plain villages
nodes.full: Survey and excavation on the Dhamar plain traced dozens of small Bronze Age farming settlements exploiting runoff from the surrounding slopes. Their check-dams and field walls are the technological seed of the hydraulic agriculture the Sabaeans later scaled to the Marib Dam.
nodes.src: the Dhamar Survey Project — T. J. Wilkinson, C. Edens, McGuire Gibson; Wilkinson and Edens, 'Survey and excavation in the central highlands of Yemen', Arabian Archaeology and Epigraphy 10 (1999).

nodes.label: Al-Midamman, a Bronze Age centre on the Tihama
nodes.full: Near the Red Sea shore, al-Midamman combined a field of standing stones, a bronze workshop casting axes and daggers on site, and an industry making granite grinding-stones for trade along the coast. It is the type-site for the Tihama's own Bronze Age, distinct from the highland villages.
nodes.src: Edward J. Keall, Royal Ontario Museum Tihama Coastal Survey; Keall, 'Possibilities for a maritime cultural landscape... al-Midamman', and annual reports in the Proceedings of the Seminar for Arabian Studies (1998–2005).

nodes.label: Sabir (Maʿlayba), the great Tihama town
nodes.full: Spread over roughly a square kilometre of mudbrick housing behind the Aden coast, Sabir supported thousands of people on sorghum agriculture, fishing and trade across the mouth of the Red Sea. Its distinctive pottery defines the 'Sabir culture', the largest second-millennium settlement known anywhere in Arabia.
nodes.src: Burkhard Vogt and Alexander Sedov, 'The Sabir culture and coastal Yemen during the second millennium BC', Proceedings of the Seminar for Arabian Studies 28 (1998); Buffa and Vogt, subsequent Maʿlayba reports.

nodes.label: The tomb ridgelines as a landscape of competition
nodes.full: The turret tombs cluster on the skylines between grazing territories, not at random. Their excavators read them as a segmentary pastoral society marking and defending access to scarce water and pasture through monument-building rather than through any recorded warfare.
nodes.src: McCorriston, 'Pilgrimage and Household in the Ancient Near East' (2011); RASA territorial-signalling models. No named battle or enemy survives — the inference is from tomb placement.

nodes.label: The bronze weapon hoards of al-Midamman
nodes.full: Al-Midamman produced groups of cast bronze axes, daggers and spearheads deposited together. Whether they are votive offerings, a smith's stock, or caches hidden against raiding is unresolved — but they are the densest concentration of Bronze Age weaponry in South Arabia.
nodes.src: Keall, ROM Tihama Coastal Survey reports; Giumlia-Mair et al., metallurgical study of the al-Midamman bronzes, in Proceedings of the Seminar for Arabian Studies (2002).

nodes.label: Sabir contracts and is abandoned
nodes.full: By the end of the second millennium the largest town in Arabia had emptied. The excavators cannot yet fix the cause — a weakening monsoon, a shifting coastline cutting off its harbour, or competition from the rising highland polities — but Sabir's fall sits exactly at the threshold of the literate Sabaean period.
nodes.src: Vogt and Sedov, PSAS 28 (1998); Buffa and Vogt on the Maʿlayba sequence. The handoff to the emerging kingdom of Sabaʾ is this folio's framing.

nodes.label: Cattle-skull deposition as a corporate act
nodes.full: The forty-odd animals in the Kheshiya ring came from many separate herds, meaning dispersed households pooled livestock and labour for one event. It is the earliest archaeological evidence in South Arabia of decision-making above the level of a single family — an incipient territorial society.
nodes.src: McCorriston et al., American Anthropologist 114 (2012); the corporate-cooperation reading is the excavators' own.

nodes.label: The turret tombs as boundary infrastructure
nodes.full: Chains of tombs along the plateau edges delimit the grazing territories of pastoral clans, tying lineage identity to a specific stretch of land. They function as property markers and social memory at once, maintained across dozens of generations.
nodes.src: Harrower and McCorriston, RASA synthesis; comparison drawn by the project to the funerary-avenue landscape of northwest Arabia.

nodes.label: The first floodwater irrigation in the highland wadis
nodes.full: Bronze Age villages in the highlands built low stone barriers to slow wadi floods and spread the silt-laden water across fields. Small and local, this runoff farming is the technique — and the organisational habit — that the kingdom of Sabaʾ would later scale up into the monumental irrigation works of Marib.
nodes.src: Michael Harrower, 'Water Histories and Spatial Archaeology: Ancient Yemen and the American West' (2016); Dhamar Survey Project, Wilkinson and Edens (1999).

nodes.label: Sabir's monumental architecture and zoned quarters
nodes.full: At its centre Sabir had a large mudbrick platform building set apart from the ordinary housing, with the settlement laid out in distinguishable zones around it. This is the earliest public architecture and planned settlement known in South Arabia, four centuries before the first royal inscriptions.
nodes.src: Vogt and Sedov, PSAS 28 (1998); Buffa and Vogt, 'The Sabir Culture and the coastal plain of the Republic of Yemen', later Maʿlayba reports.

nodes.label: The South Arabian cattle cult
nodes.full: The Kheshiya skull ring, cattle bucrania in tombs, and long-horned cattle dominating the rock art together describe a religion centred on the herd — an appeal for fertility and rain expressed through the sacrifice and display of the animals a pastoral society depended on.
nodes.src: McCorriston et al., American Anthropologist 114 (2012); parallels with the cattle burials of the northeast-Arabian Neolithic and the Saharan cattle cult are drawn explicitly in the RASA literature.

nodes.label: The standing stones of al-Midamman
nodes.full: Rows of undressed monoliths, some over three metres tall, were raised in a deliberate field near the shore. This aniconic standing-stone cult — worship focused on an unworked stone rather than an image — is the South Arabian branch of the betyl tradition that recurs across pre-Islamic Arabia down to the Nabataeans.
nodes.src: Keall, ROM Tihama Coastal Survey, PSAS reports (1998–2005); the long continuity of Arabian betyl worship is a standard observation in Nabataean religious studies (Healey, 'The Religion of the Nabataeans', 2001).

nodes.label: The ancestors on the skyline
nodes.full: Burying the dead in visible ridge-top tombs kept the ancestors permanently in view of the living and bound each lineage to its territory. Tombs were reopened and reused over centuries, making them the fixed points of a mobile society's identity.
nodes.src: RASA project mortuary studies; Soviet-Yemeni Complex Expedition tomb recording (Griaznevich, Sedov).

nodes.label: Dolmen and cist burial in the highlands
nodes.full: The Bronze Age villagers of Khawlan buried their dead in stone-slab cists and small dolmens grouped into cemeteries, furnished with pottery, beads and occasional bronze. The shift from the plateau's collective turret tombs to family graves tracks the shift from mobile herding to settled village life.
nodes.src: de Maigret (ed.), 'The Bronze Age Culture of Hawlan at-Tiyal' (1990).

nodes.label: The rock art of the Yemen highlands
nodes.full: Thousands of engraved and pecked panels across the highlands show long-horned cattle, ostriches, ibex, hunters with bows, and files of human figures. The tradition runs from the Neolithic cattle-keepers into the Bronze Age, a continuous visual record of a society that left no texts.
nodes.src: Madeleine Garcia and Mounir Arbach / A. Rachad, 'À la découverte des oasis oubliées du Yémen' and the CEFAS rock-art surveys; Anati and Jung on Yemeni highland rock art.

nodes.label: Sabir Ware
nodes.full: Hand-made, dark-burnished pottery with incised geometric bands and applied knobs is the signature of the Sabir culture — consistent enough across the southern coast to be the marker archaeologists use to trace the culture's reach.
nodes.src: Buffa and Vogt, ceramic analysis in the Maʿlayba reports; Vogt and Sedov, PSAS 28 (1998).

nodes.label: The al-Midamman megalith field
nodes.full: Raising a field of multi-tonne granite monoliths on the flat coastal plain was a feat of organised communal labour visible for kilometres — the Tihama's answer to the monumental architecture that the highlands expressed through terraces and villages.
nodes.src: Keall, ROM Tihama Coastal Survey, PSAS (1998–2005).

nodes.label: Cast bronze axes, daggers and pins
nodes.full: The bronzeworkers of al-Midamman and the highland villages produced shaft-hole axes, riveted daggers and long decorated pins, some with deliberate surface patination. Metallurgical analysis shows a controlled use of arsenic and tin, not accidental alloying.
nodes.src: Giumlia-Mair, Keall et al., metallurgical study of al-Midamman bronzes, PSAS (2002); de Maigret (1990) on the Khawlan metal assemblage.

nodes.label: Cattle, sheep and goat pastoralism
nodes.full: Mobile herding was the economic base of the interior for six thousand years. Isotope work on animal teeth and the seasonality of the plateau sites show herds moved between the highland pastures in summer and the sheltered wadis in winter.
nodes.src: RASA zooarchaeology; McCorriston et al. (2012).

nodes.label: Highland terrace agriculture begins
nodes.full: The Bronze Age villages of the highlands farmed terraced plots of wheat, barley, grapes and pulses cut into the slopes — the earliest phase of the terraced agriculture that still shapes highland Yemen, and the surplus that made permanent villages possible.
nodes.src: de Maigret (ed.) (1990); Wilkinson and Edens, AAE 10 (1999).

nodes.label: Sorghum and the summer-crop economy of the Tihama
nodes.full: Sabir grew sorghum — an African summer cereal watered by the monsoon rains that fall on the coastal plain — which let a much denser population settle the Tihama than dryland herding ever could. It is the earliest sorghum cultivation known in Arabia.
nodes.src: Boivin and Fuller (2009); Sabir archaeobotanical reports (Vogt, Buffa).

nodes.label: Obsidian exchange across the southern Red Sea
nodes.full: Volcanic glass from the Yemeni highlands and from Ethiopian sources moved in both directions across the strait of Bab al-Mandab, traced to its origin by geochemical fingerprinting in Neolithic contexts. It is the earliest documented long-distance trade in the region.
nodes.src: Lamya Khalidi, 'Holocene obsidian exchange in the Red Sea region', in 'The Evolution of Human Populations in Arabia' (2010); Zarins on Tihama obsidian.

nodes.label: Marine foraging and the Tihama shell middens
nodes.full: Mounds of discarded shell along the coast record populations living on fish, shellfish and dugong long before and alongside farming. The Red Sea shore was a productive niche in its own right, not a marginal one.
nodes.src: Khalidi, Tihama coastal survey; Keall, ROM Tihama Coastal Survey; Bökönyi faunal analyses.

nodes.label: The first traces of the aromatics economy
nodes.full: Frankincense and myrrh trees grow wild in the Hadramawt and the Dhofar hills. Direct evidence for their collection and trade before the first millennium BC is still thin, but Egyptian demand for South Arabian and African incense in the Bronze Age implies the network was already turning.
nodes.src: Nigel Groom, 'Frankincense and Myrrh: A Study of the Arabian Incense Trade' (1981); the pre-first-millennium evidence is reviewed and treated cautiously by Singer (2007). Flagged: indirect.

nodes.label: The Arabian bifacial lithic tradition
nodes.full: The South Arabian Neolithic toolkit — barbed and tanged arrowheads, bifacial knives and borers, worked by fine pressure-flaking — stayed in use for thousands of years after metal appeared in the Near East, a self-sufficient technology suited to a mobile pastoral life.
nodes.src: Crassard on the Manayzah and Wadi Sana lithics; Charpentier on the Arabian bifacial tradition, in 'The Evolution of Human Populations in Arabia' (2010).

nodes.label: On-site bronze casting at al-Midamman
nodes.full: Crucible fragments, moulds and casting waste show axes and daggers were made at al-Midamman itself, using deliberate arsenical and tin bronze. It is among the earliest metal-production sites in South Arabia and the only well-documented Bronze Age workshop on the Red Sea coast of Arabia.
nodes.src: Giumlia-Mair, Keall et al., PSAS (2002); Keall, ROM Tihama Coastal Survey reports.

nodes.label: Check-dams and runoff field systems
nodes.full: Low stone barriers thrown across wadi beds slowed the seasonal floods and let their silt settle on the fields — a small-scale technique for turning erratic rain into a crop. Sabaʾ would inherit it and scale it up into the sluices and embankments of the Great Dam of Marib.
nodes.src: Harrower, 'Water Histories and Spatial Archaeology' (2016); on the later Marib scale-up, Brunner and the DAI Marib Dam studies.

nodes.label: The granite grinding-stone industry
nodes.full: Al-Midamman quarried and shaped granite querns and hand-grinders in quantity, well beyond local need, and traded them along the Tihama. Specialised production for exchange is itself a marker of an economy past pure subsistence.
nodes.src: Keall, ROM Tihama Coastal Survey, PSAS (1998–2005).

nodes.label: Obsidian across the Bab al-Mandab
nodes.full: The oldest long-distance exchange in the region ran across the twenty-mile strait: highland-Yemeni obsidian reached the African coast and Ethiopian obsidian reached the Tihama and the highlands, a maritime connection older than farming on either shore.
nodes.src: Khalidi, 'Holocene obsidian exchange in the Red Sea region' (2010).

nodes.label: The Tihama–Horn of Africa interaction sphere
nodes.full: Sabir and al-Midamman pottery shares vessel forms and decoration with the Gash Group of the Sudanese–Eritrean lowlands and with sites near the Gulf of Tadjoura. The Bronze Age Red Sea was a single cultural sphere straddling both shores, not a boundary.
nodes.src: Andrea Manzo, 'Italian archaeological expedition to the Sudan... the Gash Delta'; Fattovich on Red Sea cultural interaction; Keall on Tihama–African ceramic links.

nodes.label: African crops move into Arabia
nodes.full: Sorghum — and in the following centuries finger millet and cowpea — crossed from Africa into the Arabian summer-rainfall zone, part of a two-way biological exchange across the Red Sea that also moved Near Eastern wheat and barley south.
nodes.src: Boivin and Fuller, Journal of World Prehistory 22 (2009).

nodes.label: Egypt, Punt and the Red Sea incense trade
nodes.full: Egyptian seaborne expeditions to the 'God's Land' of Punt for incense, myrrh, gold and ebony are recorded from Sahure to Hatshepsut's famous voyage of about 1470 BC. Whether Punt reached across to the South Arabian coast or lay only on the African side is still argued, but the aromatics network it tapped was already Bronze Age.
nodes.src: the Punt reliefs in Hatshepsut's mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari; the location debate — Kitchen for both shores, Meeks and others for Africa only.

nodes.label: The Holocene Humid Period in the south
nodes.full: A stronger Indian Ocean monsoon filled highland lakes, ran the wadis year-round and pushed vegetation deep into what is now desert. This wet window is the environmental setting for the whole South Arabian Neolithic.
nodes.src: Anne-Marie Lézine, palaeolake and pollen records from Yemen; the Qunf and Hoti cave speleothem records from neighbouring Oman (Fleitmann et al.) anchor the regional monsoon history.

nodes.label: Aridification and the retreat to the highlands
nodes.full: As the monsoon weakened, people concentrated where water persisted — the highland catchments, the perennial wadis of the Hadramawt, the springs of the Tihama. The distribution of historic Yemen's population was set by this contraction.
nodes.src: Lézine, Yemeni palaeoenvironmental syntheses; Parker and Rose on the wider Arabian mid-Holocene aridification.

nodes.label: The two South Arabias diverge
nodes.full: By the late Bronze Age the terraced-village highland world of Khawlan and the sorghum-farming coastal world of Sabir were distinct societies — different crops, different architecture, different pottery. The split between highland and Tihama Yemen persists into the present.
nodes.src: synthesis of Vogt and Sedov (1998) and de Maigret (1990).

nodes.label: The thread continues — Sabaʾ and the caravan kingdoms
nodes.full: This folio stops at 1200 BC because the evidence thins here, not because the history does. Within a few centuries the highland irrigation communities coalesce around the oasis of Marib into the kingdom of Sabaʾ, monumental dam-building begins, and Ancient South Arabian writing appears.
nodes.src: a forward reference: the successor folio south-arabia-1200bc-300bc (the early Sabaean and Minaean period) is planned but not yet built.

nodes.label: The mobile pastoral majority
nodes.full: For most of this span most South Arabians were herders who built no permanent houses. They survive as tomb clusters, hearth scatters and stone-tool debris across the plateau — a population visible as a landscape pattern rather than as families or names.
nodes.src: RASA project; the same caution the project applies against reading a mobile society as an empty one.

nodes.label: The people of Sabir
nodes.full: Several thousand people lived at Sabir farming sorghum, fishing the coast and trading across the strait, drawing on both Arabian and African connections. They are the nearest thing this folio has to a named, describable community — and their town was abandoned within living memory of the first Sabaean inscriptions.
nodes.src: Vogt and Sedov, PSAS 28 (1998); Buffa and Vogt, Maʿlayba reports.
